artifacts.summary: Two-layer allocation-staleness fix: archive-aware base-mode Check 12 plus base-mode uniqueness promotion in validate-state.sh, and a mutex-scoped --allocate-into primitive in state-write.sh, covered by the suites that own each subject and redeployed clean.

completion_data.completion_summary: Added an archive-aware base-mode counter-staleness check and promoted project_number uniqueness to base mode in validate-state.sh, added a mutex-scoped --allocate-into allocation primitive (stale-counter refusal plus counter-advance assertion) to state-write.sh, covered both in their owning test suites (70 and 14 fixtures/cases respectively, all green), fixed a pre-existing D6 fixture regression the new check surfaced, and redeployed the source store to RESULT=landed_verify_clean with the full 37-gate verify-deploy.sh passing.

memory_candidates.content: When a new validate-state.sh check or an existing check's base-mode promotion needs test coverage before the next deploy, resolve the validator via a dedicated source-store-first candidate list (e.g. C12_VALIDATOR_CANDIDATES = [source-store path, deployed path]) grepped for that check's own identifier string (e.g. "Check 12"), info-SKIPping loudly when absent -- never test against the generic $VALIDATOR, whose candidate order is deployed-first and will silently exercise the stale pre-promotion deployed copy, false-passing a regression test. This is the established pattern across ARCHIVE_VALIDATOR/D5_VALIDATOR/FS_VALIDATOR/SCOPE_VALIDATOR/D6_VALIDATOR in test-validate-state.sh.

To compute both a bound value and which of several candidate arrays supplied it in exactly one jq invocation (rather than one call per array plus bash comparison logic), build an array of {name, val} objects -- one per candidate array's own max expression -- and pipe through `max_by(.val) | "\(.val)\t\(.name)"`, read via `IFS=$'\t' read -r val name < <(jq -r '...')`. Keeps a multi-source bound computation at one jq call per file even when the message needs to name which source won.

To prove a new test assertion actually exercises the production logic it claims to (not a tautology), temporarily neutralize the specific guarded condition in the production script (e.g. replace `if $cond then ... else error(...)` with `if true then ...`, or replace an assertion's `if` body with `if false; then`), re-run the suite and confirm ONLY the expected case(s) newly fail, then restore from a byte-for-byte backup and `diff -q` to confirm the restore was exact before re-running the full suite green. This negative-control technique caught nothing wrong here but is cheap insurance and matches this codebase's own 'Negative-control checks' convention in plan Testing & Validation sections.
